title: Bounding Box Extraction for Shaded Grid Squares
approach_explanation: The problem requires finding the smallest bounding box containing all shaded squares ('*') in a given 2D grid of size $n \times m$. The approach reads the grid and records the coordinates $(j, i)$ of every shaded square. It then iterates over these coordinates to find the minimum and maximum row indices ($min\_y$, $max\_y$) and column indices ($min\_x$, $max\_x$). Finally, it extracts and prints the subgrid bounded by these extreme coordinates.

code_breakdown.explanation: Reads dimensions $n$ and $m$, initializes the grid, and iterates through each cell. When a shaded square ('*') is encountered, its column and row indices are stored as a pair in a vector.
Iterates through the collected coordinates of the shaded squares to find the minimum and maximum horizontal ($x$) and vertical ($y$) limits.
Loops through the row range from $min\_y$ to $max\_y$ and column range from $min\_x$ to $max\_x$, printing the characters of the extracted bounding box row by row.

complexity_analysis.time_justification: The algorithm reads the entire $n \times m$ grid once. Finding the minimum and maximum coordinates takes $O(k)$ time where $k$ is the number of shaded squares ($k \le n \cdot m$). Printing the final subgrid takes proportional time to its area, which is bounded by $O(n \cdot m)$. Thus, overall time complexity is dominated by reading the input matrix.
complexity_analysis.space_justification: Storage is allocated for the 2D vector of size $n \times m$ to keep the grid in memory, along with a vector of pairs storing at most $n \cdot m$ coordinate points.

strengths: Clear and straightforward logic for finding bounding boxes.
Handles varying input sizes up to the problem constraints smoothly.
edge_cases_handled: Guaranteed at least one shaded square per problem constraints.
Grid dimensions can be as small as $1 \times 1$.
best_practices_feedback: Avoid using `#include <bits/stdc++.h>` in production code; prefer explicit headers like `<iostream>` and `<vector>`.

Use `
` instead of `endl` for faster I/O performance by avoiding unnecessary stream flushes.
Variables can be named more intuitively (e.g., matching standard $(row, col)$ notation instead of mapping $x$ to column and $y$ to row).

optimization_and_alternatives.tradeoffs: Instead of storing all coordinates in a vector and finding extrema in a second pass, we can maintain $min\_row, max\_row, min\_col, max\_col$ while reading the input. This avoids the overhead of the vector of pairs, keeping auxiliary space logic cleaner, though overall memory remains governed by the grid storage.
